title: Tiered drug interaction alerts and prescriber response: a ward-randomised trial
subtitle: Cluster randomised comparison of tiered and standard alert displays across 38 wards
statement: Drug interaction alerts fire about 21,000 times a month and 94 percent are overridden, including high-severity interactions overridden without a documented reason. A tiered display that interrupts only for high-severity interactions may improve responses to the alerts that matter, but suppressing moderate alerts could hide harmful combinations. The network needs a randomised comparison because order sets change next year, and the display can be set only by ward while prescribers rotate between wards.
whoAffected: Inpatients on 38 wards receiving interacting medicines, especially older adults with kidney impairment; prescribers who face the alerts; the medication safety pharmacists who review harm.
whatHurts: A high-severity interaction overridden without thought can cause serious harm; two harm reports last year followed such combinations. Constant low-value alerts waste prescriber time and teach them to click through.
currentPractice: Every interaction of any severity interrupts the prescriber with a modal alert; overrides need a free-text reason that is rarely completed.
whyNow: The vendor can enable tiering per ward, the harm reports have raised concern, and next year's order set change would confound a before-and-after comparison.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients are protected from dangerous interactions because prescribers notice and act on the alerts that matter.
summary: Problem framed as a randomised comparison of alert displays with a harm safeguard for suppressed alerts.
